k-1.x_notes: Strengths: 10 problems, all mathematically correct (traps 3,6,9,...; Ben's take-2 opening wins only at 5, 8, 11; {1,2,3} traps are multiples of 4; misere traps 1,4,7,...; two-pile cases including the non-obvious (1,4) second-player win). Concrete actions on drawn piles ('circle the counters you take, or cross out the pile'). Good development from small piles to traps 1-20, a greedy-opening test, a rule change, two piles with a mirror-strategy question, and a misere twist, so the band will not run out of work. Header and footer follow the house format; no Name fields. Weaknesses: Problem 6 (list every way a 4- or 5-counter game can go) is off the strategy kernel, and its extra rows (8 and 10 for 5 and 8 sequences) suggest wrong counts. In Problem 8 the '1st 2nd' labels sit directly under the two piles, so they read like pile labels. The 1-20 trap tables are bare numerals, and the last page is mostly blank.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: very concrete pictures: a rules box showing take 1 and take 2, trap boxes with counters drawn, a branching diagram for 'partner takes 1 / partner takes 2' (answering every reply), and a crossed-out game record where the first player's mistake (row 3, at 5 counters) is the unique answer. The open 'find a trap above 12 and above 20' and a two-pile set with the non-obvious (4,1) second-player win are both correct. Clear go-first/go-second answer buttons. Weaknesses: the opening is dumbed down (P1 asks whether you can take the last counter this turn, P2 is one yes/no, P6 is one circle). Traps go only to 12. There is no misere game and no mirror explanation. A Name field appears on every page, the header lacks the activity title, and the footer is missing.
k-1.reason: X gives kindergartners more real thinking and a longer arc (traps to 20, greedy test, mirror strategy, misere) in the house format. Y's diagrams for 'answer every reply' and 'find the mistake' are excellent, but its first page is too thin, and the Name fields and missing title and footer break the organizer's rules.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: an accessible {1,2} entry, then claim-testing that is concrete and correct (Lee's complement-to-3 works, Mo's 10->8 fails; with {1,3,4}, Jo's 10->7 is right and Kai's 12->8 is wrong). Full 1-20 classification records a winning move in each box. Large piles 30/50/61/100 need the period-7 pattern (L, W take 1, W take 3, L). Also a {1,3,5} parity problem with explanation, a two-pile {1,2} problem with a mirror explanation, and an excellent open inverse problem: design a rule whose losing piles are the multiples of 5 (needs 1-4, plus optional extras like 6). Ample workspace, clean format. Weaknesses: there is no explicit invitation to play first. In Problem 7 the 'First Second' labels sit under the piles and are ambiguous. Only one equal-pile example supports the 'same size' question.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: focused on {1,3,4} as the outline suggests. It starts with play at 6, then 1-20 W/L. Two greedy/copycat claims are both correctly false (5: taking 4 loses; at 8 copying fails). The game-record analysis (turns 2 and 3 are the mistakes), a plan for 14 against every reply, big piles 23/28/33/50/100, and {1,3,5} with 'describe all losing piles' are all good. Two-pile {1,3,4} includes the deep (6,4) second-player case. Weaknesses: the P5 wording ('could have taken a different number and been sure to win') literally also includes turns 4 and 6, where an alternative winning move existed, so answers will be disputed. The (6,4) case is very hard for this band without values. Name fields on every page, header without activity title, no footer.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are strong and correct in substance. X has more variety, clearer named claims to test, and a rich open design problem, all in the required format. Y has a wording ambiguity in its game-record problem and the Name fields and missing title and footer.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: the {1,3,4} table to 24 leads to 100/1000/2026 (L; take 4; take 1 or 3). Four-rule comparison: {1,2} and {1,2,4} both give multiples of 3, {1,4} gives 0,2 mod 5, {1,3,5} gives evens. The greedy test across games is correct: only {1,3,5} always works. A periodicity proof for {1,3,4}. A complete-list problem for subsets of 1-6 with multiples-of-4 losing ({1,2,3} plus optional 5 and/or 6). Misere comparison shows a shift by 1. Two-pile grids for {1,2} (stripes, mirror argument) and {1,3,4} (unequal losing pairs 1-3, 1-8, 3-8, 2-7, 4-6) set up Grundy ideas concretely. The recording surfaces let kids work without asking. Clean format. Weaknesses: there is no Sprague-Grundy definition and no general pigeonhole argument for every move set. The 81-cell grid is laborious.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: mathematically deep and correct. A greedy question with a surprising finite answer (greedy wins only from 1,3,4,6,11). All odd move sets containing 1 match {1,3,5}. The {1,2,m} generalization holds for m not a multiple of 3. {1,6,9} shows a preperiod (period 5 starting at 10). The general eventual-periodicity proof and mex values for {1,3,4} lead to two-pile positions (6,4 and 12,5 lose; 5,1 and 11,3 win) and an explanation. This covers kernels 2 and 3 fully. Weaknesses: proof- and text-heavy with little concreteness; it opens with 'describe and explain why for every size' and never invites play. The variable-m problem and the pigeonhole proof will need constant adult mediation. Definition boxes sit on the student page. Name fields, missing title and footer.
grades-4-5.reason: Close call. Y goes further into Grundy values and general periodicity, but X's tables and grids give the three children concrete, self-running work that still reaches periodicity proofs, rule comparison and two-pile structure, and X follows the page format.

overall.reason: X is the better packet in every band, by a modest margin each time. It is consistently concrete, correct and varied, and follows the organizer's header and footer rules with no Name fields. Y has excellent individual problems (the reply tree and mistake-finding at K-1, the greedy and {1,6,9} questions at 4-5), but it opens K-1 with trivial items, has an ambiguous game-record question in 2-3, leans abstract at 4-5, and breaks the format on every page.
